name: Two-way table
quote: These data can be displayed in a two-way table (also called a contingency table).
plain_en: table cross-tabulating two categorical variables

name: Marginal frequencies
quote: The row sums and column sums above are called marginal frequencies.
plain_en: row and column totals in a two-way table

name: Marginal relative frequencies
quote: The row sums and column sums above are called marginal relative frequencies.
plain_en: row and column proportions in a two-way table

name: Conditional relative frequencies
quote: Conditional relative frequencies are the relative frequencies for a specific part of the table, for example, the cell frequencies in a row divided by the total for that row or the cell frequencies in a column divided by the total for that column.
plain_en: proportions within one row or column

name: Segmented bar chart
quote: Segmented bar charts are like pie charts, except that the data set is represented by a rectangular bar rather than a circle.
plain_en: bar divided into proportional category segments

name: Association
quote: Because the distributions of focus levels are different for each picture viewed, we say that the two variables, focus level and pictures viewed, are associated.
plain_en: two variables are related

name: Mosaic plot
quote: Mosaic plots are another graphical display that show the cell frequencies in a two-way table.
plain_en: area-based display of two-way table frequencies

name: Simpson’s paradox
quote: This problem is an example of Simpson’s paradox, where a conjecture can be reversed when several different groups of data are combined to form a single group.
plain_en: association reverses when groups are combined

name: Probability
quote: Even though we may not be able to foretell a specific result, we can sometimes assign what is called a probability to indicate the likelihood that a particular event will occur.
plain_en: likelihood that an event occurs

name: Event
quote: An event is a collection of one or more outcomes.
plain_en: set of one or more outcomes

name: Relative frequency (probability)
quote: The relative frequency of an event is the proportion of times the event happened—that is, the number of times the event happened divided by the total number of trials.
plain_en: proportion of trials in which event occurs

name: Law of large numbers
quote: The law of large numbers states that when an experiment is performed a large number of times, the relative frequency of an event tends to become closer to the true probability of the event; that is, probability is long-run relative frequency.
plain_en: long-run relative frequency approaches true probability

name: Gambler’s fallacy
quote: The idea that a few outcomes will immediately be balanced by other outcomes is also called the gambler’s fallacy.
plain_en: belief that past outcomes must balance soon

name: Complement
quote: The probability that an event will not occur, that is, the probability of its complement, is equal to 1 minus the probability that the event will occur.
plain_en: event not occurring

name: General addition rule
quote: The general addition rule: P(A or B or both) = P(A union B) = P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) – P(A ∩ B).
plain_en: probability of either event minus overlap

name: Mutually exclusive
quote: A and B are mutually exclusive if A ∩ B = ∅ or, equivalently, P(A ∩ B) = 0.
plain_en: events that cannot occur together

name: General multiplication rule
quote: The general multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A intersect B) = P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B|A).
plain_en: probability of both events using conditional probability

name: Independent events
quote: A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A) or, equivalently, P(B|A) = P(B).
plain_en: one event does not change the other's probability

name: Conditional probability
quote: Conditional probabilities shrink the population of interest.
plain_en: probability given that another event occurred

name: Random variable
quote: If X represents the different numbers associated with the potential outcomes of some chance situation, we call X a random variable.
plain_en: numerical outcome of a chance process

name: Expected value
quote: The expected value or mean of a discrete random variable X is given by μ X = E(X) = ∑ xP(x), where P(x) is the probability of outcome x.
plain_en: probability-weighted average outcome
covers_concepts: Expected value; Mean of a random variable

name: Weighted average
quote: The expected value is sometimes referred to as a weighted average.
plain_en: average weighted by probabilities

name: Variance of a discrete random variable
quote: If we regard the (x − μ)2 terms as the values of some discrete random variable (whose probability is the same as the probability of x), the mean of this new discrete random variable is ∑(xi − μx)2pi, which is precisely how we define the variance, σ2, of a discrete random variable:
plain_en: probability-weighted average squared deviation

name: Adding variances of independent random variables
quote: Variances of independent random variables can be added together, but standard deviations cannot!
plain_en: independent variances add but standard deviations do not

name: Probability distribution
quote: A probability distribution is a list or formula that gives the probability of each outcome.
plain_en: list or formula of outcome probabilities

name: Binomial setting
quote: We have a binomial setting when the following conditions are met: ■There are two possible outcomes, often referred to as success and failure. ■There are a fixed number of trials, n. ■The trials are independent; that is, the outcome of one trial does not affect the outcome of any other trial.
plain_en: fixed independent trials with two outcomes

name: Binomial random variable
quote: The binomial probability function refers to a binomial random variable X with n independent trials and probability of success p.
plain_en: count of successes in binomial trials

name: binompdf
quote: binompdf (n, p, x) gives the probability of exactly x successes in n trials, where p is the probability of success on a single trial.
plain_en: calculator probability of exactly x successes

name: binomcdf
quote: binomcdf (n, p, x) gives the cumulative probability of x or fewer successes in n trials, where p is the probability of success on a single trial.
plain_en: calculator probability of at most x successes

name: Mean of a binomial distribution
quote: The expected value or mean number of successes is np.
plain_en: expected successes equals n times p

name: Shape of a binomial distribution
quote: The shape of a binomial distribution is skewed right when p < 0.5, symmetric when p = 0.5, and skewed left when p > 0.5.
plain_en: binomial shape depends on success probability

name: Probability distribution (function)
quote: A probability distribution is a function, table, or graph that links outcomes of a statistical experiment with its probability of occurrence.
plain_en: function linking outcomes to probabilities

name: Cumulative probability distribution
quote: A cumulative probability distribution is a function, table, or graph that links outcomes with the probability of less than or equal to that outcome occurring.
plain_en: probability of at most a given outcome

name: Normal distribution
quote: One bell-shaped distribution, called the normal distribution, is valuable for providing a useful model in describing various natural phenomena.
plain_en: bell-shaped symmetric probability model

name: Points of inflection
quote: There is a point on each side where the slope is steepest. These two points are called points of inflection, and the distance from the mean to either point is precisely equal to one standard deviation.
plain_en: curve points one standard deviation from mean

name: Normal parameters
quote: Every normal distribution is completely determined by two parameters: its mean μ and its standard deviation s.
plain_en: mean and standard deviation define a normal curve

name: Empirical rule
quote: The empirical rule (also called the 68-95-99.7 rule) applies specifically to normal distributions. About 68% of the values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95% of the values lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean, and about 99.7% of the values lie within 3 standard deviations of the mean.
plain_en: 68, 95, and 99.7 percent within 1, 2, 3 SDs

name: Standard normal distribution
quote: normalcdf(lowerbd, upperbd) = probability between two z-scores for the standard normal distribution (mean = 0 and SD = 1)
plain_en: normal distribution with mean zero and SD one

name: normalcdf
quote: normalcdf(lowerbd, upperbd, mean, SD) = probability between two raw scores for a normal distribution with the given mean and SD
plain_en: calculator normal probability between two values

name: invNorm
quote: invNorm(probability) = z-score with the given probability to the left for the standard normal distribution (mean = 0 and SD = 1)
plain_en: calculator value with given left probability

name: Normal approximation to the binomial
quote: A general rule of thumb is that the normal is a good approximation to the binomial whenever both np and n(1 − p) are at least 10.
plain_en: use normal when np and n(1-p) are large

name: Sampling distribution
quote: The probability distribution showing how a statistic varies is called a sampling distribution.
plain_en: distribution of a statistic over samples

name: Central limit theorem
quote: The following principle, called the central limit theorem of statistics (abbreviated CLT), forms the basis of much of what we discuss in this and the following units. Start with a population with any shape distribution whatsoever. Pick n sufficiently large (at least 30), and take all samples of size n. Compute the mean of each of these samples. Then the set of all sample means is approximately normally distributed.
plain_en: sample means become normal for large samples

name: Mean of the sampling distribution of x̅
quote: the mean μ x̅ of the sampling distribution of x̅ equals the population mean μ.
plain_en: sample mean averages to population mean

name: Standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̅
quote: the standard deviation σ x̅ of the sampling distribution of x̅ equals the population standard deviation σ divided by the square root of the sample size.
plain_en: population SD divided by square root n

name: Randomization distribution
quote: One example of a sampling distribution is a randomization distribution, a collection of statistics generated by simulation.
plain_en: simulated distribution created by random reassignment

name: Binomial distribution
quote: The binomial probability function refers to a binomial random variable X with n independent trials and probability of success p.
plain_en: distribution of successes in fixed independent trials
